title: thousands evacuate washington wildfires 2026 08 04
text:
Aug 4 (Reuters) - Hello,
Today’s newsletter is all about the wildfires, heatwaves and drought gripping the Northern Hemisphere.
The wildfires raging in the United States on the outskirts of Spokane, Washington, have destroyed at least 700 buildings and forced tens of thousands of people to flee their homes, officials said.
The Spokane Area Fire, which includes three separate blazes, was threatening the areas under evacuation orders, Spokane Fire Chief Tom Williams told Reuters.
The blazes ranked as the top firefighting priority in the U.S., including the drought-parched Pacific Northwest, where dozens ​of major wildfires have burned for weeks, degrading air quality across a wide region.
‘The worst natural disaster in our region’
Enormous palls of smoke billowed into the sky north of the city, as flames devoured forest land ‌6 miles (10 km) from Spokane's downtown.
The fires have burnt more than 8,000 acres (3,200 hectares) since erupting on Saturday on the northern fringe of the city, home to about 230,000 residents west of the Rocky Mountain foothills near the Idaho border.
No injuries or fatalities have been reported so far, according to Benjamin Cossel, a spokesperson for the incident command center.
"There's a high probability that will change in the coming days" as flames subside and search teams are able to reach devastated communities still inaccessible due to extreme fire activity.
Spokane Mayor Lisa Brown called it "the worst natural disaster our region has faced."
Washington Governor Bob Ferguson said he ​had spoken with U.S. President Donald Trump on Sunday and requested assistance from the Federal Emergency Management Agency. The governor has declared a statewide emergency.
‘We don't want to scare you’
Kami Fehlig, 58, was one of hundreds of area residents who ​fled for their lives before wind-driven flames engulfed their homes over the weekend.
Picking through charred ruins of her house in search of keepsakes, Fehlig paused on Monday to recount how she and ⁠her husband watched in disbelief as fire jumped the narrow Spokane River and swept toward their parkside neighborhood in the city's northwest on Saturday.
"About 30 minutes before it jumped the river, my husband and I were seeing how bad it was, and we told ​the kids, 'We don't want to scare you, but we think you should start preparing to grab some things.'"
Only later did they learn that their house, as well as the family's chicken coop, had burned to the ground, along with much of their surrounding community.
At least 700 ​structures have gone up in flames, mostly in residential areas, and aerial infrared surveys showed that possibly another 400 buildings, including homes, had been damaged or destroyed, Cossel said.
The cause of the blazes was under investigation.
Talking Points
In Conversation
Phil Duffy, chief scientist at a U.S.-based science-driven nonprofit, Spark Climate Solutions, shares his thoughts on rising global temperatures:
"Over the past 25 years, Earth's energy imbalance – how much ​heat the planet absorbs rather than releasing ⁠into space – has more than doubled, meaning global warming is accelerating.
"Climate models show far smaller increases than observations do, suggesting the models policymakers and businesses rely on may significantly underestimate future warming."Understanding what is driving these dynamics is an urgent scientific priority.
"Human-caused greenhouse gas emissions and reduced particulate pollution both contribute, but more research is needed – and the scientific community studying Earth’s energy imbalance remains small and under-resourced."Satellite monitoring is also at risk. The U.S. once operated six space-based monitoring instruments; only four remain, likely dropping to two within a year.
"NASA's Libera instrument is planned ⁠to launch next ​year, but the agency estimates a 75% chance of a data gap before 2040, which would severely limit our ability to track Earth's heat uptake and more ​accurately project future warming."
ESG Lens
Climate insurance: The wildfires have renewed attention on Europe's "protection gap" – the difference between total losses from disasters and the amount covered by insurance. The European Central Bank and the European Union's insurance regulator have warned that only a quarter of losses from climate-related catastrophes between 1980 and 2024 were insured. Wildfire ​insurance is also less developed in Europe than in the United States. Click here for the full Reuters analysis.
